The Maestro · Part 2 · Phase 0 · 🔬 Researcher + 🧠 ML engineer hats

Proving It Small

A toy on a laptop is not evidence about real models. Before he raises money or rents a cluster, Gopala needs two things: a training stack he trusts, with loss that falls predictably as models grow, and a fair test of whether verified skills help a real language model. This part builds both. The trainer and the scaling-law fit are real code with real output from a laptop CPU; the real-model experiments are written as runnable scripts with fixed protocols and decision rules, priced at a few thousand dollars of rented GPU time.

1. Mission log: weeks 4–8

Week 4 · The trainer
  • Writes a 150-line GPT trainer from scratch rather than starting from a big framework, so he understands every line he will later scale (section 3).
  • Smoke-tests it on his laptop; finds and fixes an initialisation bug that made the first loss value absurd.
Week 5 · The ladder
  • Trains four sizes on the same data, fits a scaling law, and checks the fit predicts the largest model from the three smaller ones (sections 4–5).
  • Rents one GPU for two days to repeat the ladder at 10–100× the size (section 6).
Weeks 6–8 · The real test (in parallel with Part 3's planning)
  • Builds a 300-task suite from design-partner-style problems, split by repository so test tasks never share code with skill sources.
  • Rents one 8-GPU node in short bursts: serves an open 7–8B model with vLLM, runs the retrieval test (H1) and the LoRA comparison (H2).
  • Applies the decision rules written before the runs (sections 7–9).

2. Two questions

Two questions, two kinds of evidence

❓H1Do curated skills help a real model at inference time?
🧪TestPaired comparison on the same tasks, with a confidence interval
❓H2Do verified skills help when trained into the weights?
🧪TestLoRA fine-tune vs base on held-out tasks

Phase 0 must answer both cheaply before any large money is spent.

Track A · Can he train?Does his own training code work, and does loss fall predictably with model size? Without this, every later decision about model size is a guess.
Track B · Does the idea hold?Do verified skills help a real language model on held-out tasks (H1)? Does folding them into weights beat generic data (H2)?
  • Both tracks are cheap on purpose.
    • The start-up playbook makes the point that experiments usually cost several times the final run
      • the cheapest experiments are the ones that kill bad ideas early.

3. A trainer you trust

  • The trainer is deliberately small: a GPT-style decoder (pre-norm blocks, causal attention through PyTorch's fused scaled_dot_product_attention, which uses FlashAttention-style kernels on a GPU), byte-level tokens so no tokenizer is needed yet, AdamW, a warmup-then-cosine learning-rate schedule, gradient clipping, bf16 on GPUs, periodic validation and checkpoint-and-resume.
    • Those last features look like luxuries on a laptop
      • on a cluster they are what separates a lost hour from a lost week (running the Llama 3 run).
train_tiny.py · PyTorch · CPU or one GPU
"""train_tiny.py — a minimal GPT trainer for the Maestro's small-scale proofs.

The same file trains a 0.1M-parameter smoke-test model on a laptop CPU and,
unchanged, a 125M–1B model on one rented GPU (multi-GPU comes in Part 9).
Features that matter later: cosine schedule with warmup, bf16 autocast, gradient
clipping, periodic eval, and checkpoint/resume so a crashed run loses minutes.

  python3 train_tiny.py --size xs --steps 400          # CPU smoke test
  python3 train_tiny.py --size 125M --steps 20000 --bs 64 --ctx 1024 --lr 6e-4   # one GPU
"""
import argparse, glob, math, os, time
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

SIZES = {  # name: (layers, heads, d_model) — params grow ~12·L·d²
    "xs": (2, 2, 64), "s": (4, 4, 128), "sm": (4, 4, 192), "m": (6, 8, 256),
    "125M": (12, 12, 768), "350M": (24, 16, 1024), "1B": (24, 16, 2048),
}


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.proj, self.h = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d), h
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.ln1(x)).split(C, dim=2)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.h, C // self.h).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))
        y = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)   # FlashAttention on GPU
        x = x + self.proj(y.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C))
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))


class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab, ctx, L, H, D):
        super().__init__()
        self.tok, self.pos = nn.Embedding(vocab, D), nn.Embedding(ctx, D)
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(Block(D, H) for _ in range(L))
        self.ln, self.head = nn.LayerNorm(D), nn.Linear(D, vocab, bias=False)
        self.head.weight = self.tok.weight                            # weight tying
        self.apply(self._init)

    @staticmethod
    def _init(m):                                                      # GPT-2 style: small init
        if isinstance(m, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(m.weight, std=0.02)
        if isinstance(m, nn.Linear) and m.bias is not None:
            nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        x = self.tok(idx) + self.pos(torch.arange(idx.shape[1], device=idx.device))
        for b in self.blocks:
            x = b(x)
        logits = self.head(self.ln(x))
        loss = None if targets is None else F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), targets.flatten())
        return logits, loss


def load_text():
    """Byte-level data: any local text. Default: the Python standard library source."""
    root = os.path.dirname(os.__file__)
    files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(root, "*.py")))[:120]
    data = b"".join(open(f, "rb").read() for f in files)
    t = torch.tensor(list(data), dtype=torch.long)
    n = int(0.95 * len(t))
    return t[:n], t[n:]


def batch(data, bs, ctx, gen):
    ix = torch.randint(len(data) - ctx - 1, (bs,), generator=gen)
    x = torch.stack([data[i:i + ctx] for i in ix])
    return x, torch.stack([data[i + 1:i + ctx + 1] for i in ix])


def lr_at(step, total, peak, warm):
    if step < warm:
        return peak * (step + 1) / warm
    return peak * 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * (step - warm) / max(1, total - warm)))


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--size", default="xs"); ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=400)
    ap.add_argument("--bs", type=int, default=16); ap.add_argument("--ctx", type=int, default=128)
    ap.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=3e-3); ap.add_argument("--ckpt", default="ckpt_tiny.pt")
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    torch.manual_seed(a.seed); gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(a.seed)
    dev = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
    train, val = load_text()
    L, H, D = SIZES[a.size]
    model = GPT(256, a.ctx, L, H, D).to(dev)
    n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) - model.pos.weight.numel()
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=a.lr, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.1)
    start = 0
    if os.path.exists(a.ckpt):                                        # resume after a crash
        s = torch.load(a.ckpt, map_location=dev)
        model.load_state_dict(s["model"]); opt.load_state_dict(s["opt"]); start = s["step"]
    tokens = a.steps * a.bs * a.ctx
    print(f"size={a.size} params={n_params/1e6:.2f}M tokens={tokens/1e6:.2f}M "
          f"compute≈{6*n_params*tokens:.2e} FLOPs device={dev}")
    t0 = time.time()
    for step in range(start, a.steps):
        for g in opt.param_groups:
            g["lr"] = lr_at(step, a.steps, a.lr, warm=max(1, a.steps // 20))
        x, y = batch(train, a.bs, a.ctx, gen)
        with torch.autocast(dev, dtype=torch.bfloat16, enabled=dev == "cuda"):
            _, loss = model(x.to(dev), y.to(dev))
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True); loss.backward()
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0); opt.step()
        if step % 100 == 0 or step == a.steps - 1:
            model.eval()
            with torch.no_grad():
                vl = sum(model(*(t.to(dev) for t in batch(val, a.bs, a.ctx, gen)))[1].item() for _ in range(8)) / 8
            model.train()
            print(f"step {step:5d}  train {loss.item():.3f}  val {vl:.3f}  ({time.time()-t0:.0f}s)")
            torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), "opt": opt.state_dict(), "step": step + 1}, a.ckpt)
    print(f"final_val {vl:.4f} params {n_params}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
  • The first smoke test printed an initial loss of about 33, far above the ~5.5 expected for random guessing over 256 byte values (ln 256 ≈ 5.55).
    • The cause: PyTorch's default embedding initialisation combined with tied input and output weights produced huge logits.
    • The fix is the GPT-2-style small initialisation in _init.

After it, the smoke test behaves:

$ python3 train_tiny.py --size xs --steps 400 size=xs params=0.12M tokens=0.82M compute≈5.73e+11 FLOPs device=cpu step 0 train 5.486 val 5.432 (0s) step 100 train 2.724 val 2.559 (1s) step 200 train 2.479 val 2.304 (3s) step 300 train 2.206 val 2.332 (4s) step 399 train 2.187 val 2.332 (5s) final_val 2.3317 params 116480

Real output. The biggest model was worse until its learning rate was lowered: one setting does not fit all sizes.

  • Next, four sizes from about 0.1M to 4.8M parameters, each trained for 1,500 steps on the same 3.1M tokens of Python source, with the same learning-rate recipe.
    • Same data, same steps: the only thing that changes is the model size, so the curve isolates the effect of size.
ladder.sh
#!/bin/sh
# ladder.sh — train four sizes on the same data budget, collect "params loss" for scaling_fit.py
rm -f ladder.txt ckpt_*.pt
for size in xs s sm m; do
  python3 train_tiny.py --size $size --steps 1500 --ckpt ckpt_$size.pt | tee log_$size.txt
  grep final_val log_$size.txt | awk '{print $4, $2}' >> ladder.txt
done
python3 scaling_fit.py ladder.txt
$ sh ladder.sh # same 3.07M tokens and 1,500 steps for every size, lr 3e-3 size=xs params=0.12M ... final_val 1.8097 size=s params=0.83M ... final_val 1.5734 size=sm params=1.83M ... final_val 1.4943 size=m params=4.80M ... final_val 1.6173 ← the biggest model is WORSE $ python3 train_tiny.py --size m --steps 1500 --lr 1e-3 # rerun with a smaller learning rate size=m params=4.80M tokens=3.07M compute≈8.86e+13 FLOPs device=cpu ... final_val 1.4991

5. Fitting a scaling law

What the scaling-law fit says

1.450loss floor in the fit
−0.604exponent on parameters
1.410 vs 1.499predicted vs measured for the largest model
0.0147fit error (RMSE) on 4 runs

Real output of scaling_fit.py. Fitting on three points over-predicted the gain: small ladders extrapolate badly.

  • Scaling laws describe how loss falls as a power of model size, approaching a floor: L(N) = E + A·N−α.
    • Fitting one to small runs is how labs decide how big to go before spending real money (planning the run).

Gopala's fit uses only numpy:

scaling_fit.py · numpy
"""scaling_fit.py — fit L(N) = E + A·N^(-alpha) to a ladder of small runs.

Input: one line per run, "params final_val_loss" (the last line printed by
train_tiny.py). Output: the fitted law and a prediction for bigger models.
Uses only numpy: a grid over (E, alpha) with least squares for A.

  python3 scaling_fit.py ladder.txt
"""
import sys
import numpy as np

rows = [tuple(map(float, l.split())) for l in open(sys.argv[1]) if l.strip() and not l.startswith("#")]
N, Lv = np.array([r[0] for r in rows]), np.array([r[1] for r in rows])

best = None
for E in np.linspace(0, Lv.min() * 0.98, 200):          # irreducible loss below the best run
    for alpha in np.linspace(0.05, 1.0, 200):
        x = N ** -alpha
        A = np.dot(x, Lv - E) / np.dot(x, x)              # least squares for A given E, alpha
        err = np.mean((E + A * x - Lv) ** 2)
        if A > 0 and (best is None or err < best[0]):
            best = (err, E, A, alpha)

err, E, A, alpha = best
print(f"fit: L(N) = {E:.3f} + {A:.2f} * N^-{alpha:.3f}   (rmse {err**0.5:.4f} on {len(N)} runs)")
for n in N:
    print(f"  N={n:>10,.0f}  measured {Lv[list(N).index(n)]:.3f}  fitted {E + A * n ** -alpha:.3f}")
for n in (1e7, 1e8, 1e9):
    print(f"  predicted at N={n:.0e}: {E + A * n ** -alpha:.3f}  (extrapolation: treat with care)")
$ python3 scaling_fit.py ladder.txt # with the lr 1e-3 rerun for the largest model fit: L(N) = 1.450 + 413.06 * N^-0.604 (rmse 0.0147 on 4 runs) N= 116,480 measured 1.810 fitted 1.810 N= 826,112 measured 1.573 fitted 1.560 N= 1,828,992 measured 1.494 fitted 1.518 N= 4,804,608 measured 1.499 fitted 1.488 predicted at N=1e+07: 1.474 (extrapolation: treat with care) predicted at N=1e+08: 1.456 (extrapolation: treat with care) predicted at N=1e+09: 1.451 (extrapolation: treat with care) # predict-then-check: fit only the three smallest runs, predict the fourth 3-point fit predicts 1.410 at 4.8M parameters; measured 1.499

Measured loss and the fitted law

Real points from the ladder (log scale on size). The dashed line is the fit; beyond the last point it is extrapolation.

  • Two lessons came out of this ladder, both of which repeat at every scale.
    • First, one learning rate does not fit all sizes:
      • with the same 3e-3 as the small models, the 4.8M model trained worse than the 1.8M one
      • at 1e-3 it recovered.
    • Larger models need smaller learning rates, which is why real scaling studies tune them per size or use parameterisations that transfer them.
    • Second, the predict-then-check test failed usefully: fitted on the three smallest runs, the law predicted 1.41 for the largest model, which measured 1.50.
    • The cause is data: every run saw the same 3.1M tokens, so beyond about 2M parameters extra size buys almost nothing, and the fitted floor of ~1.45 is a property of this tiny dataset, not of the models.
    • Two cautions matter more than the numbers.
    • First, these runs hold data fixed, so bigger models are increasingly data-starved; a real plan varies both size and tokens (the Chinchilla approach).
    • Second, extrapolating two orders of magnitude from four points is risky; labs fit on dozens of runs spanning several orders of magnitude.
    • The value here is the habit: predict, then check.
    • Gopala refits with the three smallest runs and checks how well that predicts the fourth before he believes any extrapolation.

6. Moving to a real GPU

  • The same script runs unchanged on one rented GPU at 125M–1B parameters (--size 125M --ctx 1024 --bs 64), with a proper tokenizer and a slice of a public dataset such as FineWeb-Edu replacing the Python source.

What changes is not the code but the discipline:

ConcernLaptopOne rented GPU
DataLocal Python files, bytesTokenized shards of a public corpus, streamed
PrecisionFP32BF16 autocast (already in the script)
Throughput checkSeconds per stepTokens per second and MFU: compare achieved FLOP/s (6·N·tokens per second) with the GPU's peak
Failure handlingRerunCheckpoint every few hundred steps; resume automatically (already in the script)
Loggingprint()An experiment tracker; every run tagged with code version and config (research tooling)
  • Multi-GPU training (data, tensor and pipeline parallelism) waits for Part 9; for Phase 0, single-GPU runs are enough to validate the stack and the scaling behaviour.

7. H1 on a real model

  • Part 1's toy showed the shape of H1.
    • The real test uses an open 7–8B instruction model served with vLLM on one GPU, and 300 engineering tasks written in the style of the design partners' work: fix this failing test, add this feature to this function, write this data transformation.
    • Each has hidden tests.
    • Tasks are split by repository: skills may only come from training repositories, and test tasks come from repositories the library never saw, so a skill cannot simply be the answer.
skill_eval.py · needs a model server · not executed for this article
"""skill_eval.py — H1 with a real model: does retrieving verified skills help?

Runs the same coding tasks twice against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for
example an open 7–8B model served by vLLM on one rented GPU):
  arm "base":   task prompt only
  arm "skills": task prompt + the k most similar verified skills from the library
Each answer is executed against the task's hidden tests in a subprocess with a
timeout. Same model, same sampling settings, same number of attempts per task.

  vllm serve <open-model> --port 8000           # on the rented GPU
  python3 skill_eval.py tasks.jsonl skills.jsonl --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1

tasks.jsonl  : {"id", "prompt", "tests"}           (tests = Python asserts)
skills.jsonl : {"name", "code", "doc", "tests"}    (only skills that passed the gate)
NOTE: this script needs a running model server; it was not executed for this article.
"""
import argparse, json, re, subprocess, sys, tempfile
from collections import Counter
from openai import OpenAI          # pip install openai


def tokens(s):
    return Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z_]{3,}", s.lower()))


def top_k(task, skills, k=3):
    """Cheap lexical retrieval; swap in embeddings once the library is large."""
    q = tokens(task["prompt"])
    score = lambda s: sum((q & tokens(s["doc"] + " " + s["name"])).values())
    return [s for s in sorted(skills, key=score, reverse=True)[:k] if score(s) > 0]


def extract_code(text):
    m = re.search(r"```(?:python)?\n(.*?)```", text, re.S)
    return m.group(1) if m else text


def run_tests(code, tests, timeout=10):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile("w", suffix=".py", delete=False) as f:
        f.write(code + "\n\n" + tests + "\n")
    try:
        r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, f.name], capture_output=True, timeout=timeout)
        return r.returncode == 0
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        return False


def ask(client, model, prompt, n):
    out = client.chat.completions.create(model=model, n=n, temperature=0.6, max_tokens=1024,
                                         messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return [extract_code(c.message.content) for c in out.choices]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("tasks"); ap.add_argument("skills")
    ap.add_argument("--base-url", default="http://localhost:8000/v1"); ap.add_argument("--model", default="default")
    ap.add_argument("--attempts", type=int, default=4)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    client = OpenAI(base_url=a.base_url, api_key="local")
    tasks = [json.loads(l) for l in open(a.tasks)]
    skills = [json.loads(l) for l in open(a.skills)]
    wins = {"base": 0, "skills": 0}
    for t in tasks:
        arms = {"base": t["prompt"]}
        found = top_k(t, skills)
        ctx = "\n\n".join(f"# Verified skill: {s['name']}\n# {s['doc']}\n{s['code']}" for s in found)
        arms["skills"] = (f"These verified helper functions may be useful:\n```python\n{ctx}\n```\n\n" if found else "") + t["prompt"]
        for arm, prompt in arms.items():
            ok = any(run_tests(c, t["tests"]) for c in ask(client, a.model, prompt, a.attempts))
            wins[arm] += ok
    n = len(tasks)
    print(f"pass@{a.attempts}: base {wins['base']}/{n}  skills {wins['skills']}/{n}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
  • Design choices worth copying: the two arms use the same model, the same sampling settings and the same number of attempts; correctness is decided by executing hidden tests, never by a judge model; and retrieval starts deliberately simple (word overlap) so that a positive result cannot be blamed on a clever retriever.
    • Part 6 of the Agent Layer series explains why stuffing too many skills into the prompt backfires; the script caps it at three.

8. Fair statistics

Fair statistics: the paired test

124 / 300base model solves
140 / 300with skills
+0.053difference
[+0.030, +0.080]95% confidence interval

Simulated self-check of paired_ci.py (not real model results). The interval excludes zero, so the rule says proceed.

  • With 300 tasks, a few points of difference can be luck.
    • Because both arms solve the same tasks, the right comparison is paired: task by task.
    • Gopala writes his decision rule before running anything: proceed only if the 95% bootstrap interval for (skills − base) lies entirely above zero.
paired_ci.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""paired_ci.py — is the difference between two arms real, or luck?

Both arms run the SAME tasks, so compare them task by task (a paired test) and
bootstrap a confidence interval for the difference in success rate. Gopala's
rule: proceed only if the 95% interval for (skills − base) is entirely above 0.

  python3 paired_ci.py            # runs a self-check on simulated outcomes
"""
import random


def paired_bootstrap(a, b, iters=10_000, seed=0):
    """a, b: lists of 0/1 outcomes per task for arm A and arm B (same order)."""
    rng, n = random.Random(seed), len(a)
    diffs = []
    for _ in range(iters):
        idx = [rng.randrange(n) for _ in range(n)]
        diffs.append(sum(b[i] - a[i] for i in idx) / n)
    diffs.sort()
    return sum(y - x for x, y in zip(a, b)) / n, diffs[int(0.025 * iters)], diffs[int(0.975 * iters)]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Self-check with SIMULATED outcomes (not results): 300 tasks, true rates 40% vs 47%.
    rng = random.Random(1)
    base = [int(rng.random() < 0.40) for _ in range(300)]
    skills = [max(x, int(rng.random() < 0.12)) for x in base]     # skills help some tasks, rarely hurt
    d, lo, hi = paired_bootstrap(base, skills)
    print(f"simulated: base {sum(base)}/300, skills {sum(skills)}/300, diff {d:+.3f}, 95% CI [{lo:+.3f}, {hi:+.3f}]")
    print("decision:", "proceed" if lo > 0 else "not proven")
$ python3 paired_ci.py simulated: base 124/300, skills 140/300, diff +0.053, 95% CI [+0.030, +0.080] decision: proceed
  • The self-check uses simulated outcomes to show the method works; it is not a result.
    • With real outcomes, the same function decides the experiment.
Outcome (written in advance)Decision
Interval entirely above 0, gain ≥ 5 pointsProceed to H2 and to planning (Part 3)
Interval above 0, gain under 5 pointsProceed cautiously; improve retrieval and skill quality before raising
Interval includes 0Not proven: enlarge the suite or rethink the skill format; do not raise on this
Interval below 0Stop: skills hurt real models, as hoarding hurt the toy

9. H2: into the weights

  • H1 shows skills help when they are in the prompt.
    • H2 asks whether the model can carry them in its weights.
    • Two LoRA adapters on the same base, trained for the same number of examples: one on verified skills turned into task-and-solution pairs, one on an equal amount of high-quality public code.
    • Then both are evaluated without retrieval on the held-out tasks.
lora_skills.py · Hugging Face TRL + PEFT · needs a GPU · not executed for this article
"""lora_skills.py — H2 preview: fold verified skills into weights with LoRA.

Two adapters on the same open base model, trained for the SAME number of tokens:
  --data skills   verified skills turned into (task → solution) chat examples
  --data generic  an equal-size sample of high-quality public code data
Then rerun skill_eval.py WITHOUT retrieval against each adapter: if the skills
adapter wins on held-out tasks, weights absorbed something retrieval provided.

  pip install transformers peft trl datasets
  python3 lora_skills.py --base <open-model> --data skills  --out adapter-skills
  python3 lora_skills.py --base <open-model> --data generic --out adapter-generic
NOTE: needs a GPU (one 80 GB card is enough for a 7–8B model with LoRA);
it was not executed for this article.
"""
import argparse, json
from datasets import Dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer


def skill_examples(path):
    for line in open(path):
        s = json.loads(line)                       # {"name", "code", "doc", "tests", "task"}
        yield {"messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": s["task"]},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": f"```python\n{s['code']}\n```"},
        ]}


def generic_examples(path, limit):
    for i, line in enumerate(open(path)):          # {"prompt", "completion"} from a public code set
        if i >= limit:
            break
        r = json.loads(line)
        yield {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": r["prompt"]},
                            {"role": "assistant", "content": r["completion"]}]}


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--base", required=True); ap.add_argument("--data", choices=["skills", "generic"], required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--skills", default="skills_train.jsonl"); ap.add_argument("--generic", default="generic_code.jsonl")
    ap.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    skills = list(skill_examples(a.skills))
    rows = skills if a.data == "skills" else list(generic_examples(a.generic, len(skills)))
    trainer = SFTTrainer(
        model=a.base,
        train_dataset=Dataset.from_list(rows),
        peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
        args=SFTConfig(output_dir=a.out, num_train_epochs=2, per_device_train_batch_size=4,
                       gradient_accumulation_steps=8, learning_rate=1e-4, lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
                       warmup_ratio=0.03, bf16=True, logging_steps=10, save_strategy="epoch", seed=0),
    )
    trainer.train()
    trainer.save_model(a.out)
    print(f"saved {a.data} adapter to {a.out} ({len(rows)} examples)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
  • Why LoRA here and not full fine-tuning: it trains a few million parameters instead of billions, fits on one GPU, and makes the comparison cheap to repeat with different seeds.
    • The full version of this experiment, folding skills into a model during pre-training and post-training, is Phase 2's job (Parts 10–11).

10. What Gopala found (scenario)

Scenario, not measurement
  • This section continues the story.
    • The outcomes below are what the scenario assumes so the series can proceed; they are not results of running the scripts above.
    • Run them yourself to get real numbers.
  • In the scenario, H1 lands in the first row of the decision table: retrieval of verified skills improves pass@4 on held-out repositories, with a paired interval clearly above zero.
    • H2 lands in the second row: the skills adapter beats the generic-code adapter on held-out tasks, but by less, and it slightly weakens performance on a general coding benchmark, which is exactly what the gate's no-regression check exists to catch.
    • The ladder and scaling fit behave as expected.
    • Gopala's conclusion: the effect is real enough to plan around, the gate is not optional, and how skills enter the weights will need care at scale.

Verdict
  • Track A works: a 150-line trainer trains, resumes and scales predictably across a four-size ladder, and the fitted law gives a first, cautious handle on how big to go.
    • Track B has runnable, pre-registered tests for both hypotheses, with paired statistics and decision rules written before the data.
    • The scenario's results are good enough to plan around and honest enough to show where the gate matters.
